title: Embeddings, tokens, and what the model reads instead of text

videos.script: A language model never sees a letter, only a list of whole numbers. {{ids}} This lesson is about how text becomes those numbers, and what the numbers become. {{corpus}} It works on forty-five lines about a market town, written for this course. {{split}} Cut into characters, the text is long. Cut into words, every new word is a hole. {{bpe}} Byte-pair encoding finds the pieces in between, by gluing the commonest pair together, again and again. {{merges}} A real tokenizer does the same on bytes, so no text is ever unknown. {{tok}} Then each number picks a row out of a table, and that row is the token's embedding. {{lookup}} Train the table on the corpus, and the rows move. Monday ends up near Friday, and the baker near the potter. {{near}} One word's neighbours mean nothing, and the lesson shows why. {{red}} Last comes the bill: the same sentences in Portuguese cost twice the tokens. {{bill}} Context and price are both counted in tokens, so that ratio is paid on every request. {{end}}
